plan.paradox: A penny gets you a whole record collection. And you never see the bill.

plan.cause: The "penny" option is a bait; if you don't cancel by the deadline the next album ships automatically with a full-price invoice, turning the tiny upfront cost into recurring revenue that peaked at $1.4 billion in 1996 and collapsed to $17 million by 2014.
plan.everyday: A streaming service offers a free-month trial, then auto-renews at $9.99; a gym sells a $1 enrollment fee but locks you into a $30 monthly membership; a coffee shop gives a free pastry with a $0.99 signup, then bills $4.99 for the next week's drinks. In each case the cheap entry point hides an ongoing charge, so the paid plan feels like a smart upgrade.
plan.rule: Watch the fine print; a tiny upfront price often masks a larger recurring bill. Follow for more.

beats.say: A penny gets you a whole record collection. And you never see the bill.
Sign up for 12 records for a penny.
Or choose the standard club plan with regular prices.
Or pick the no-commitment digital download option.
Members must buy a minimum number of albums at regular club prices. Sounds generous.
But it does a job: it forces future purchases.
If you don't cancel by the deadline, the next album ships and you get a full-price bill.
That automatic charge kept revenue at $1.4 billion in 1996.
When the model collapsed to $17 million by 2014, the parent filed for bankruptcy in 2015.
You see it everywhere: a streaming service promises a free month, then charges $9.99 monthly.
A gym advertises a $1 enrollment, then locks you into $30 a month.
A coffee shop gives a free pastry for $0.99, then bills $4.99 for the week's drinks, making the paid plan feel like the smart choice.
Watch the fine print; a tiny upfront price often masks a larger recurring bill. Follow for more.
